solver: LS-DYNA R13.1 MPP (double precision), INSA Rennes cluster

examples.title: Concrete cylinder 150 × 300 mm — uniaxial compression
setup: Full cylinder, O-grid mesh of 16 000 hexahedra (≈ 7.5 mm), ELFORM 1 with Flanagan–Belytschko stiffness hourglass control (IHQ 4, QM 0.05).

Bottom face fixed in z; one centre node and one edge node fix rigid-body motion. Top face pushed down 3 mm (1 % strain) in 30 ms with a 0.5 ms smooth start. Platens are frictionless, so the stress state is uniaxial.
Stress = bottom reaction / (π · 75²); strain = platen displacement / 300 mm.
Every material card is the site's generator output for f'c = 30 MPa, d_max = 16 mm, ρ = 2.3 t/m³.
notes: With rate effects off, KCC, CSCM and CDP peak at 30.1, 30.3 and 30.0 MPa: the generated cards reproduce the input f'c within 1 %. The initial modulus is 31–35 GPa, close to the EN 1992-1-1 value Ecm ≈ 33 GPa.

KCC with its DIF curve peaks at 42.4 MPa (+41 %). The explicit test runs at about 0.3–1 s⁻¹, where the CEB-FIP MC90 compressive DIF for f'c = 30 MPa is 1.34–1.40, so the solver is doing what the curve asks. For quasi-static analyses set dif_model = 0 (LCRATE = 0), or use the lower fib MC2010 curve (dif_model = 2).
Winfrith has no softening branch in compression: the stress keeps rising slowly to 31.9 MPa at 1 % strain. Use it where tensile cracking governs, not for crushing.

Post-peak behaviour differs widely at 1 % strain: CDP keeps 34 % of its peak, KCC 64 %, CSCM 96 %. With frictionless platens the strain field stays uniform, so these branches are a material response rather than a localisation, and they depend on the compressive softening parameters (EFC for CDP, GFC for CSCM, b1 for KCC).
Hourglass and kinetic energy stay below 0.2 % of the external work in all five runs.

examples.title: Notched concrete prism 150 × 150 × 550 mm — three-point bending
setup: EN 14651 geometry: span 500 mm, central notch 25 mm deep and one element (4.95 mm) wide. 99 750 hexahedra of ≈ 5 mm, fully integrated (ELFORM 2). A first run with ELFORM 1 + hourglass control lost 20–55 % of the external work to hourglass energy once the crack localised, so it was discarded.
Supports and loading line are rows of nodes (three node lines at each support, two at midspan). Midspan pushed down 1 mm in 40 ms.
CMOD is the opening of the two bottom nodes at the notch edges. GF = work of the load over the deflection / ligament area (125 × 150 mm²), without the self-weight correction.
f_ct,L uses EN 14651: 3 F_L l / (2 b h_sp²), with F_L the largest load for CMOD ≤ 0.05 mm.
KCC is run without the DIF curve so that all four models are compared quasi-statically.
notes: Winfrith and CSCM give f_ct,L = 4.6 and 4.4 MPa, in the range expected for a notched prism of C30 concrete (EN 1992-1-1 flexural strength ≈ 1.45 f_ctm ≈ 4.2 MPa). KCC without rate effects peaks much lower, at 2.9 MPa, and dissipates only 0.048 N/mm: the generated tensile damage parameters (b2, b3 with the internal crack-band width) make it more brittle than the other two at this mesh size; see the open RSIZE issue in the KCC documentation. fib MC2010 would expect G_F ≈ 0.14 N/mm for f_cm = 38 MPa.

Energy from the load–deflection curve exceeds the fracture energy in the cards: Winfrith 0.125 vs 0.075 N/mm (×1.66), CSCM 0.113 vs GFT 0.08 N/mm (×1.41). The crack is one element wide in both runs, so part of the excess is damage that spreads outside the crack band and part is support indentation; the curve is not corrected for either. Calibrate G_F against a test like this one rather than trusting the input value.

The crack runs straight up from the notch tip in all models. CSCM erodes the cracked elements (ERODE = 1.05), which shows as a gap in the fringe plot; KCC and Winfrith keep the elements and localise the strain.

With ELFORM 2 the hourglass energy is zero for KCC and CSCM. Winfrith is implemented only in the one-point element (the manual says ELFORM = 1), so it keeps hourglass modes and reports 5.6 % hourglass energy. Kinetic energy stays below 0.9 % of the external work, so the 40 ms loading is quasi-static.
The CDP run is still in progress; its curve will be added when it finishes.

examples.title: Round steel bar d₀ = 10 mm — tensile test (ISO 6892-1 proportional specimen)
setup: Parallel length 80 mm, gauge L₀ = 50 mm = 5.65 √S₀. O-grid mesh of 8 000 hexahedra (≈ 1 mm), ELFORM 2. The diameter is reduced by 0.5 % at mid-length, so the neck forms in the gauge length.
One end fixed, the other pulled 24 mm in 60 ms (about 5 s⁻¹ in the gauge length). Mass scaling to Δt = 1E-4 ms affects only the smallest elements.
Engineering stress = reaction / (π · 5²); engineering strain = change in the gauge length / 50 mm.

All three models describe the same S355 steel: MAT_024 uses the Yun & Gardner (2017) curve for f_y = 355 and f_u = 510 MPa. MAT_003 (SIGY 355.6, ETAN 1646) and MAT_015 (A 355.6, B 1137, n 0.822, C 0) are least-squares fits to that curve, made for this example.
notes: All three fits start yielding at 351–353 MPa at 0.2 % strain, so the elastic–plastic transition is consistent.

MAT_024 with the Yun & Gardner curve gives R_m = 504 MPa (input f_u = 510) at A_g = 17.9 % (Yun & Gardner predict 18.2 %). The neck forms at the reduced section and the load then drops, as in a real test.

MAT_003 (bilinear) and MAT_015 (Johnson–Cook) never neck within 30 % strain: their hardening stays above the Considère limit (dσ/dε ≥ σ), so the engineering stress keeps rising to 606 and 546 MPa. A least-squares fit that matches the curve well up to f_u still over-predicts strength beyond it. Use MAT_024 with a measured true-stress curve when necking or ductile failure matters, or fit MAT_003/MAT_015 only up to A_g and add a failure criterion.
No failure strain is defined, so the neck in MAT_024 thins without fracture. Add FAIL (MAT_024) or a damage model (e.g. *MAT_ADD_DAMAGE_GISSMO) to predict elongation at fracture A.
